about: Numbers and news for laporteweathernow.com/amazon (Amazon Rainforest Watch). Updated weekly from official data as reported by trusted outlets. Only numbers the sources state; calm, factual, no hype.
headline: Forest clearing is down in Brazil. Drought, fire and illegal gold mining are the dangers now.

now.title: A record El Niño could bring drought
now.text: Brazil's Geological Service gives a 69% chance that this El Niño becomes stronger than any since 1950. It expects above-normal heat, less rain and three to five heat waves from September to November, with Rio Negro basin rivers below normal and dropping more in November. The El Niño should last into early 2027. Drought is what lets fire burn through standing forest.

source.label: Revista Cenarium, citing the Geological Service of Brazil

now.title: Illegal gold miners enter a protected reserve in Peru
now.text: Peru's prosecutors say illegal gold miners have entered Tambopata National Reserve in the Madre de Dios region. A three-day operation destroyed 56 motors, 78 mining rafts and more than 13,000 gallons of fuel. Mercury from the mining poisons rivers and the fish Indigenous communities depend on.

now.title: Deforestation alerts at their lowest since 2013
now.text: Brazil's space agency, INPE, counted 2,874 square kilometers of deforestation alerts in the Amazon from August 2025 through July 2026, down 36% and the lowest since 2012–13. Scientists caution that logging, drought and fire can still damage standing forest without counting as clearing.

now.title: Illegal mining still earns billions in Brazil
now.text: A Greenpeace investigation found illegal gold mining in Brazil's Amazon still brings in billions of dollars despite federal crackdowns, concentrated in Indigenous lands such as the Yanomami territory. High gold prices and weak tracing of where gold comes from keep it going.
